awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Stability and Instability of Periodically Stationary Nonlinear Waves with Applications to Fiber Lasers
awd_abstract_narration:
Since the introduction of the soliton laser in the 1990's researchers have developed several generations of short pulse, high energy fiber lasers for a variety of applications. These lasers are configured to produce periodically stationary pulses by propagating light many times around a loop. Although different physical effects change the shape of the pulse as it traverses the loop, the pulse returns to the same shape once each period (round trip). A significant challenge for the modeling of these lasers is that from one generation to the next there has been a dramatic increase in the amount by which the pulse breathes, necessitating novel mathematical approaches. This project will develop theoretical and computational methods to determine periodically stationary pulse solutions of nonlinear wave equations modeling laser systems and to analyze their stability (robustness in the presence of random noise and other system perturbations). The project will provide computational tools to aid in the design of high energy lasers for medical applications, and of frequency combs for highly accurate measurements of time and frequency, with applications to geo-location systems, time and frequency standards, the calibration of astronomical instruments, and trace gas sensing. The project will provide broad training in applied mathematics for doctoral students and mentoring for junior faculty. In addition, the project will support complementary activity focused on pedagogical innovations. 
 
The laser models to be studied in this project are based on variants of the cubic-quintic complex Ginzburg-Landau equation. Classically, the spectrum of a stationary nonlinear wave is given by the zero set of the Evans function of the linearized differential operator. The stability of periodically stationary solutions of the Ginzburg-Landau equation and of models of fiber lasers will be characterized in terms of the spectrum of the monodromy operator of the linearization about the pulse. Since the stability problem for time-periodic solutions is formulated on a cylinder, rather than on the real line, any generalization of the Evans function will involve Fredholm determinants of operators on infinite-dimensional function spaces rather than classical determinants of matrices. To avoid the extreme stiffness of the differential equations used to compute the Evans function in this infinite dimensional context, the point spectrum of the monodromy operator will be identified with the zero set of an infinite-dimensional Fredholm determinant of a Birman-Schwinger operator on an infinite cylinder. Numerical methods will be developed to compute Fredholm determinants of such Birman-Schwinger operators. These methods will then be employed to determine stability regions in design parameter space for periodically stationary solutions of the Ginzburg-Landau equation and of models of experimental fiber laser systems. The generic instability of stationary solutions of reaction diffusion equations has recently been established by applying a related topological invariant called the Maslov index to the spectral theory of self-adjoint operators. A novel version of the Maslov index will be used to establish general stability results for periodically stationary solutions of the Ginzburg-Landau equation.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Since the mid 1990's engineers have developed several generations of short-pulse, high-energy fiber lasers for applications to geo-location systems, ultra-precise measurement of time and frequency, the calibration of astronomical instruments, attosecond science, and trace gas sensing. In these systems, pulses of light circulate around a loop consisting of several components such as optical fibers, amplifiers, filters, and saturable absorbers. While each of these components changes the shape of the pulse as it propagates, to be useful in applications, the system must be designed so that the pulse returns to the same shape once each round trip.

In this project we  developed mathematical models to simulate the periodic evolution of pulses in such laser systems. To do so, we designed new computational algorithms to discover periodic pulses and to determine their stability in the presence of noise and other random perturbations. Because prior work on pulse stability assumed that the pulse is stationary, maintaining its shape as it propagates, we had to develop new theoretical approaches to tackle the stability problem for periodic pulses. The stability of a periodic pulse is characterized by the spectrum of the monodromy operator of the pulse, which consists of the essential spectrum and the eigenvalues. We derived a theoretical formula for the essential spectrum and a computational method for the eigenvalues that is based on a matrix discretization of the monodromy operator. We applied this new methodology to determine the stability of periodic pulses in a model of an experimental fiber laser system.

A classical method for determining the stability of stationary pulses is to compute the Evans function, which is a matrix determinant whose zeros are the eigenvalues. Because the Evans function involves the solution of a system of differential equations which exhibits different behaviour at different scales, an Evans function probably does not exist for periodic pulses. To overcome this obstacle, we showed that, for stationary pulse solutions of the Ginzburg-Landau equation, the Evans function determinant is equal to the Fredholm determinant of an associated integral operator. We developed a numerical method to compute the Fredholm determinant, justified the method with theoretical convergence results, and validated the method using numerical simulations. These results point the way forward to a viable, theoretically justified computational approach for  determining the stability of periodic pulse solutions of nonlinear wave equations.

 Three graduate students received training in computational and applied mathematics as part of the project. The project also resulted in a new partnership within the framework of IMPRESSU, an NSF initiative aimed to foster collaboration between Ukrainian, USA and eastern European scholars.

A major broader impact of the project focused on training of teams of undergraduate learning assistants who worked alongside graduate teaching assistants in the active learning problem sections for a Calculus III course coordinated by the Principal Investigator at the University of Texas at Dallas. Working in small groups, students engage in mathematical reasoning, solve problems with their fellow students, and explain their thinking. The undergraduate learning assistants interact with the groups by asking probing questions designed to improve the students' conceptual understanding and mathematical communication skills. The learning experiences of 870 students were positively impacted by the 47 undergraduate learning assistants who assisted with the course.
